planting.note: Plant nursery-grown divisions in spring into consistently moist, sunny to lightly shaded meadow or rain-garden soil; Tightlips is a selected garden form of nodding ladies' tresses valued for its narrow, tightly furled flower shape.

directions: Tightlips is a selected form of the widespread nodding ladies' tresses, chosen by specialty growers for its unusually narrow, tightly furled flowers that hold a slim, tubular shape rather than the more open, flared lip typical of wild populations. Like the species, it sends up spiraling white flower spikes in late summer and fall and thrives in consistently moist, sunny to lightly shaded meadow or rain-garden soil. Because it is propagated from nursery stock rather than wild-collected, it establishes more reliably than most native terrestrial orchids and can slowly form colonies by offset growth. Keep the planting site evenly moist through the growing season, since reliable fall bloom depends on consistent soil moisture.

planting.note: Plant nursery-grown divisions in spring into consistently moist meadow or rain-garden soil in full sun to light shade; Wake Up is a selected garden form of spring ladies' tresses chosen for its early seasonal bloom.

directions: Wake Up is a selected form of spring ladies' tresses chosen by specialty growers for its early, reliable flowering, opening its spiral spikes of small white flowers ahead of typical wild-type plants each season. It favors the same consistently moist meadow or rain-garden soil as the species, performing best where competing vegetation is kept low and light shade tempers the hottest part of the day. Propagated by division rather than wild collection, it establishes more readily than most native terrestrial orchids and rewards patient gardeners with an earlier start to the native-orchid bloom season. Avoid letting the planting site dry out in summer, and leave established clumps undisturbed once they take hold.

planting.note: Set out tubers or nursery divisions in early spring into consistently moist, humus-rich soil in partial shade to open sun; northern marsh orchid is a compact, cold-hardy Dactylorhiza well suited to cooler climates.

directions: Northern marsh orchid produces dense, cylindrical spikes of rich magenta-purple flowers above narrow, unspotted leaves, flowering in late spring to early summer from damp grassland, dune slacks, and marsh habitats across northern Britain and Ireland. It is one of the more compact and cold-tolerant Dactylorhiza species, tolerating cooler, shorter growing seasons better than some of its larger relatives. Plant tubers or nursery divisions into consistently moist, humus-rich soil in partial shade to open sun, avoiding sites that dry out in summer. Top-dress lightly with leaf mold each autumn and leave established clumps undisturbed, since the tubers and their mycorrhizal partners are easily disrupted by digging.

planting.note: Plant divisions in early spring at their original depth into moist, humus-rich, low-fertility soil in dappled shade; Bressingham Bonus is a registered (1991) selection sold under the fuchsii name, though its larger stature suggests some Dactylorhiza elata parentage.

directions: Bressingham Bonus is a registered garden selection carrying noticeably heavier, denser flower spikes than a typical common spotted orchid, with pale pink to lilac blooms marked with darker loops and dashes above spotted leaves; some growers consider it a probable hybrid with the taller Dactylorhiza elata rather than a pure fuchsii selection. It shares the species' preference for dappled shade at a woodland edge or in open meadow turf with moist, well-drained, humus-enriched soil. Plant divisions in early spring at their original depth, disturbing roots as little as possible, since the orchid depends on an intact mycorrhizal partnership in the surrounding soil. Protect emerging spotted leaves from slugs in early spring and avoid high-fertility soils, which favor foliage over flowering.

planting.note: Plant divisions in early spring at their original depth into moist, humus-rich, low-fertility soil in dappled shade; Claire is a named selection of the common spotted orchid chosen for its large, well-marked pale pink flowers.

directions: Claire is a named garden selection of the common spotted orchid, chosen by specialty growers for unusually large, well-marked pale pink flowers held above the typical mottled, spotted leaves. It is grown under the same conditions as the species, favoring dappled woodland-edge or meadow sites with moist, humus-rich, low-fertility soil. Set divisions out in early spring at their original planting depth and avoid disturbing the roots, since established clumps rely on a delicate mycorrhizal association that does not tolerate transplanting well. Mulch lightly with leaf mold each year rather than fertilizing to keep the soil in the lean condition this orchid prefers.
